passages.happening:
Jesus tells his disciples a story. A rich man hears that his manager has been wasting his property. He calls him in: ‘Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer’ (verse 2).

The manager thinks fast. ‘I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg’ (verse 3). He decides to make friends who will take him into their homes when he is out of work. So he calls in his master's debtors one by one. The first owes a hundred measures of olive oil. ‘Take your bill,’ says the manager. ‘Sit down quickly, and write fifty’ (verse 6). The next owes a hundred measures of wheat. ‘Take your bill and write eighty’ (verse 7).

“The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly. For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light” (verse 8).

Then Jesus says, “I tell you, use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves, so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story, and it is the hardest of all Jesus' parables. Readers have argued over it for centuries. It helps to see first what is clear, and then what is not.

What is clear. Rich landowners often lived far from their land and left a manager in charge. The manager collected rents and debts, made loans and signed contracts in his master's name. Many of the debts were owed in goods, not coins: olive oil and wheat. A hundred measures of either was a large amount, the trade of a big estate, not a family's groceries. So the manager is giving away a great deal.

He is caught wasting his master's goods and told he is finished. He has very little time before his last day. He cannot dig, he will not beg, and so he uses the one thing he still has, his authority over the bills, to put the debtors in his debt. When he is out on the street, they will owe him a welcome.

Then comes the surprise. The master praises him. Not for his honesty: the story calls him ‘the dishonest manager’. He praises him because he ‘acted shrewdly’. Shrewd means quick to see what is coming and wise enough to act on it now.

What is not clear is exactly what the manager did when he changed the bills. Scholars have offered three main answers, and each has its strength and its hard question.

One answer: he simply cheated his master a second time, giving away what was not his, and the master, like a man who admires a clever rogue, could only tip his hat. The strength of this reading is that the story itself calls him dishonest, even after the bills are changed. Its hard question is why Jesus would build a lesson on a fraud. Those who hold it answer that Jesus does this elsewhere, as with the unjust judge (18:1-8): if even a rogue plans ahead for his future, how much more should God's people?

A second answer: he cut out his own share. On this reading, the manager had added his own fee or commission to each bill. By writing the bills down, he gave up his own profit, not his master's property. The strength of this reading is that it explains why the master did not object. Its hard question is that the story never mentions a fee, and still calls him dishonest.

A third answer: he cut out hidden interest. The Law of Moses forbade Israelites to charge one another interest on loans (Deuteronomy 23:19). Some think lenders hid interest by writing a loan of goods as a larger amount than was really lent. Removing it would make the master look law-abiding and generous, and he could hardly complain. The strength of this reading is that it fits the Law. Its hard question is that, as critics reply, the amounts cut do not match what is known of interest rates, and the story does not say the debtors were Jews.

Scholars have not agreed, and these notes do not choose. Whichever reading is right, the story turns on one thing the manager saw clearly: his time was short, and what he did with money now would decide where he stood later.
passages.ot:
The Law commanded open hands toward the poor: “you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs” (Deuteronomy 15:8). It forbade making a profit from a poor neighbour's need: “If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest” (Exodus 22:25).

And Proverbs teaches that how we treat the poor is how we treat God: “Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him” (Proverbs 14:31).
passages.hard:
Is Jesus praising dishonesty? No. The master in the story praises the manager's shrewdness, and the story still calls him dishonest. Jesus' own lesson comes in verse 9, and it is not ‘cheat your employer’. It is a comparison from the lesser to the greater. People who live only for this age are often wiser about it than God's people are about eternity. They plan, they act quickly, they use what they have to secure their future. Jesus asks his followers to be at least that clear-eyed.

What does verse 9 mean, then? ‘Worldly wealth’ is literally ‘the mammon of unrighteousness’. Mammon is an Aramaic word that meant wealth or property; it was not the name of a god. Many readers think ‘of unrighteousness’ does not mean stolen money, but money as it belongs to this passing, unjust age. Money will run out (‘when it is gone’). So use it now for people: give it, share it, make friends with it, above all among the poor, who cannot repay (14:13-14). Those friends, in the age to come, will be glad to see you. Jesus is not saying that money can buy a place in heaven. He is saying that what you do with money shows where your heart is (12:34), and that it can be turned into something that lasts.

What Jesus draws from the story is clear, whatever the manager did: use money for people, and do it while there is time.
passages.asks: The manager saw that his time was short and acted. Ask whether you live as if your money and your time will last for ever. Then ask one practical question: whose life could your money make better this month, especially someone who could never pay you back?

passages.happening:
Jesus goes on. “Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much” (verse 10).

If you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will trust you with true riches? If you have not been faithful with what belongs to someone else, who will give you something of your own?

“No servant can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
These sayings turn the parable around. The manager was not faithful; he was only clever. Jesus now asks for both.

‘Very little’ is money. Jesus calls money a small thing, even though it seems so large to us. The ‘true riches’ are the things of God's kingdom. And money is ‘the belongings of another’: what we have is lent to us by God, and we are his managers, as the man in the story was the rich man's.

‘Serve’ here means to work as a slave. A slave belonged to one master, and two owners would pull him in two directions. Jesus speaks of money as a master who wants to be served. The word is the Aramaic mammon again, meaning wealth or property, not the name of a god. But Jesus speaks of it as a rival lord.

Matthew gives the same saying about two masters in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:24). Luke places it right after the story of the manager, so that its meaning is plain: money is either your servant, used for God and for others, or it is your master.
passages.ot: Israel's Scriptures warned against trusting wealth: “He who trusts in his riches will fall” (Proverbs 11:28). And the first commandment allowed no rival: “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3).
passages.hard:
Is money evil? No. The Bible does not say money is evil; Paul writes that “the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10), not money itself. Jesus speaks here of service: whom you work for, whom you obey when the two pull apart. You can have money without serving it. But you cannot serve it and God at once.

This is not a call to despise people who have money either. Luke's book shows women of means supporting Jesus from what they owned (8:3), and later a rich tax collector, Zacchaeus, finding salvation as he gives (19:8-9). The question Luke puts to every reader, rich or poor by the world's measure, is where their treasure is.
passages.asks: Look at how you used money last week. Ask who it served. And ask whether there is a ‘little’ thing, an expense report, a small debt, a borrowed item, where you are not quite faithful. Jesus says the little things show what we will do with much.

passages.t: The Law, the kingdom, and divorce
passages.happening:
The Pharisees, “who were lovers of money” (verse 14), hear all this and sneer at Jesus.

He says to them, “You are the ones who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is prized among men is detestable before God” (verse 15).

“The Law and the Prophets were proclaimed until John. Since that time, the gospel of the kingdom of God is being preached, and everyone is forcing his way into it” (verse 16). Yet “it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a single stroke of a pen to drop out of the Law” (verse 17).

“Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery, and he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Luke says these Pharisees loved money. That is a charge against the men who sneered that day, not a description of every Pharisee. The Pharisees were a movement of devout Jews who tried to keep God's law in the whole of ordinary life (see the note on 11:37-44). So ‘Pharisee’ is not a word for a hypocrite. In later Christian speech it came to mean that, but it did not mean that to Jesus' hearers. Many in Jesus' day, as now, took wealth as a sign of God's approval. Jesus says God looks at the heart, and that what people admire may be what God finds hateful.

Verses 16 to 18 can seem to jump from one subject to another. They are linked by the Law. John the Baptist marks a turning point: the time of promise in the Law and the Prophets has given way to the good news of the kingdom. But that does not mean the Law is thrown away. The ‘stroke of a pen’ is the smallest mark a scribe could make. Jesus is saying that God's word is not careless in any part.

Then, as an example of the Law's lasting demand, Jesus speaks of divorce. In his day a Jewish husband could send his wife away with a written notice (Deuteronomy 24:1), and teachers argued about what reasons were good enough. Jesus' saying is stricter than either side. It also protects the wife: the husband who sends her away to marry someone else is the one who commits adultery against her. Mark and Matthew give longer accounts of this teaching (Mark 10:1-12; Matthew 19:1-9).
passages.ot:
God's judgment of the heart is an old teaching: “the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

On marriage, Jesus goes back to the beginning, as he does in Mark: “a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). And the prophet Malachi warned husbands who were sending away their wives: “So guard yourselves in your spirit and do not break faith” (Malachi 2:16).
passages.hard:
What does ‘everyone is forcing his way into it’ mean? The Greek verb can be read more than one way. Some read it as praise: eager people, tax collectors and sinners among them, are pressing into the kingdom with all their strength. Others read it as ‘everyone is urged insistently to come in’, like the servant in 14:23. Matthew's form of the saying sounds more like a warning of violence against the kingdom (Matthew 11:12). Careful scholars still differ, and these notes do not settle it.

Does verse 18 mean divorce and remarriage are never allowed? Christians answer in different ways, and each answer is held by careful readers. The Catholic Church teaches that a true sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved while both spouses live, though it allows separation and can declare that a true marriage never existed. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be for life but, as an act of mercy, allow a second marriage with a service of repentance. Most Protestant churches read Matthew's words ‘except for sexual immorality’ (Matthew 19:9) and Paul's words about a spouse who leaves (1 Corinthians 7:15) as showing that unfaithfulness and desertion can free the innocent partner to remarry. Many also count abuse as breaking the marriage covenant. Some scholars argue that Jesus allowed separation but not remarriage. These notes do not decide between them.

What all of them share is Jesus' main point. God meant marriage to last for life, and divorce is always a tearing of what he joined.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

If you have been through a divorce, this verse is not a door closed in your face. Jesus spoke these words to men who were sending their wives away to suit themselves. Many who read them now were the ones sent away, or tried for years to save a marriage that broke. God knows your heart (verse 15).
passages.asks: Jesus says God knows the heart, behind what we show other people. Ask what you most want to be admired for, and whether God would admire it too. And if marriage is part of your life, ask how you can keep faith with your husband or wife this week, in small things.

passages.happening:
There was a rich man “dressed in purple and fine linen, who lived each day in joyous splendor” (verse 19). At his gate lay a beggar named Lazarus, covered with sores, longing to eat the scraps that fell from the rich man's table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.

The beggar died, and the angels carried him to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried. “In Hades, where he was in torment, he looked up and saw Abraham from afar, with Lazarus by his side” (verse 23).

He called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue. For I am in agony in this fire’ (verse 24).

But Abraham answered, ‘Child, remember that during your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things. But now he is comforted here, while you are in agony’ (verse 25). And a great chasm has been fixed between them, so that no one can cross from one side to the other.
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story.

Purple cloth was dyed with a costly dye made from sea snails. It took thousands of them to dye one garment, and purple was the colour of kings and the very rich. Fine linen was costly cloth too. And the rich man feasted not on special days but every day.

Lazarus lay at his gate, perhaps carried there and left by others. A gate like this led into the courtyard of a great house; the rich man passed him whenever he went in or out. Dogs in that world were not pets but street scavengers. Their licking his sores shows how helpless he was: he could not even keep them away.

Apart from Abraham, the father of Israel, Lazarus is the only person Jesus names in any of his parables. His name is a form of Eleazar, which means ‘God has helped’. No one else helped him. The rich man has no name at all. (He is sometimes called ‘Dives’, but that is only the Latin word for ‘rich’.)

Then death reverses everything. Lazarus is carried by angels to ‘Abraham's side’, literally Abraham's bosom or chest. At a feast, a guest lay beside another and leaned against him, as the beloved disciple did with Jesus at the Last Supper (John 13:23). So Lazarus, who longed for crumbs, now has the place of honour at the feast, next to the father of God's people. The rich man, who feasted daily, is buried, and then he is in Hades in torment.

‘Hades’ is the Greek word that the Greek Old Testament used for Sheol, the place of the dead. It is not the same word as Gehenna, which Jesus uses elsewhere for final judgment. Jewish writings from before Jesus' time pictured the dead kept in separate places until the judgment; one of them, the book called 1 Enoch, speaks of a bright spring of water for the righteous. Stories of a rich man and a poor man whose places are reversed after death were also told elsewhere, among them an old Egyptian tale. Jesus may be using a picture his hearers already knew, and giving it his own ending.
passages.ot:
The prophets saved some of their sharpest words for the rich who feasted while the poor suffered: “You lie on beds inlaid with ivory, and lounge upon your couches,” said Amos, “but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph” (Amos 6:4, 6). Ezekiel said the sin of Sodom was this: “She and her daughters were arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49).

The Law had told Israel, “For there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11). And Proverbs warned, “Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, he too shall cry out and receive no answer” (Proverbs 21:13). The rich man cries out, and receives no answer.
passages.hard:
What was the rich man's sin? Not that he was rich. Abraham himself was rich (Genesis 13:2), and he is the one at the feast. The rich man's sin is that Lazarus lay at his gate. He saw him every day; he even knows his name (verse 24). He never once fed him. His wealth did not damn him. His closed hand did. So the story does not teach that the poor are saved because they are poor, or that the rich are lost because they are rich. Luke's point, as his book page puts it, is not that being poor makes anyone good, or that being rich makes anyone bad. It is that God sees the one at the gate, and asks us to see him too.

It does not teach the opposite either. Some preachers say that wealth is a sign of God's favour, and poverty a sign of too little faith. This story turns that upside down. The man whom everyone would have called blessed was the one in danger.

Is this a parable, or an account of real people? Luke does not call it a parable, and Lazarus has a name, so some readers have taken it as a true story. Most read it as a parable. It begins like the parables around it, ‘There was a rich man’ (compare 16:1), and it uses pictures, a finger, a tongue, a chasm, that are hard to take as a plain map of the unseen world.

What does it teach about the dead? Christians hold different views. Many hold that the dead are conscious between death and the resurrection, and they point to this story, to Jesus' words to the dying criminal, “today you will be with Me in Paradise” (23:43), and to Paul's longing to “depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). Others hold that the dead sleep until the resurrection, and read this story as using a picture its hearers knew to make a point about wealth and Scripture. Christians also differ on what final judgment is like, and these notes do not settle that here. What the church confesses together is the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come.

So it is wise not to build a geography of hell on this story, or to use its fire to frighten anyone, a child least of all. Jesus did not tell it to scare. He told it to wake people up while there was still time to open their hands. Its plain teaching is enough: God sees the poor, what we do in this life matters beyond it, and there comes a time when it is too late to change.
passages.asks: Who lies at your gate? Not far away, in another country, but near enough that you pass them often: a neighbour, a classmate, a man on the corner, a family in your church who is struggling. Ask whether you know their name. Then ask what one open-handed thing you could do for them this week.

passages.t: ‘Even if someone rises from the dead’
passages.happening:
The rich man begs again. ‘Then I beg you, father, send Lazarus to my father's house, for I have five brothers. Let him warn them, so that they will not also end up in this place of torment’ (verses 27-28).

Abraham replies, ‘They have Moses and the prophets; let your brothers listen to them’ (verse 29).

‘No, father Abraham,’ he says, ‘but if someone is sent to them from the dead, they will repent’ (verse 30).

Abraham answers, ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead’ (verse 31). The story ends.
passages.hearers:
Even now the rich man treats Lazarus as a servant to be sent on errands: ‘send Lazarus’. He has not really seen him yet.

He does love his brothers, and that is to his credit. But he thinks they need something more than they already have: a miracle, a visitor from the dead. Abraham says they have enough. ‘Moses and the prophets’ means the Scriptures of Israel. They already said, again and again, open your hand to the poor. The brothers do not need more evidence. They need to listen.

Luke's readers would not miss the last line. Someone did rise from the dead: Jesus himself. And not everyone was persuaded. When the women told the apostles the tomb was empty, “their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women” (24:11). On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus began “with Moses and all the Prophets” to explain what the Scriptures said about himself (24:27). The Scriptures and the resurrection point to the same Lord.
passages.ot: The brothers already have the Law, which said, “you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs” (Deuteronomy 15:8). They have the prophets, who asked, “Isn’t it to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him?” (Isaiah 58:7). Abraham's answer is that the Scriptures are enough to show anyone how to live.
passages.hard:
Does this mean miracles are useless? Not quite. Luke is full of signs, and the resurrection is at the centre of the faith. But a sign cannot force a heart open. A person who has decided not to obey what they already know will find a way to explain away even a resurrection. The problem with the five brothers is not too little evidence. It is too little willingness.

This is a hard word for anyone, believer or skeptic, who says, ‘If God would only show me a sign, I would change.’ The honest question is whether we are living by the light we already have.
passages.asks: The rich man wanted a messenger from the dead. Abraham pointed to the book his brothers already owned. Ask what you already know you should do, from Scripture or from your own conscience, and have not done. You do not need another sign to begin.
